Fit hypothesis based on read pages: Both price by monthly pageview tier rather than a flat fee: Fathom runs from $15/month for up to 100,000 pageviews to $470/month for up to 25,000,000 (Custom above that), while Plausible's Starter/Growth/Business tiers list $9/$14/$19/month at the 'up to 10k pageviews' slider position before scaling separately by site and seat count. Fathom bundles at least 50 sites into every tier, visible together in one all-sites view, whereas Plausible's Starter plan includes only 'One site' and Growth only 'Up to 3 sites.' Neither source describes Plausible's cookie use, so that part of the original framing is not supported here.

Source
Source
Source

Original discovery hypothesis, unverified: The closest head-to-head pick for a buyer who wants a flat-fee, cookieless, single-dashboard tool across multiple sites instead of Plausible's pageview-tiered pricing.

They promise: That a visitor can get clear, understandable website analytics without being tracked by cookies or having their privacy invaded — 'Analytics without the cookies.'

Pricing: Usage-tiered by monthly pageviews shared across all sites on the account, not flat-fee: $15/month up to 100,000 pageviews, $25/month up to 200,000, $45/month up to 500,000, $60/month up to 1,000,000, $100/month up to 2,000,000, $140/month up to 5,000,000, $200/month up to 10,000,000, $290/month up to 15,000,000, $380/month up to 20,000,000, $470/month up to 25,000,000, and Custom above that. Every tier includes at least 50 sites and the same feature set; yearly billing gets 2 months free; extra site packs of 50 cost $10/month (or $100/year) each, up to 15 packs.
Way in: 7-day free trial (card required; card is not charged until the trial ends and they email before billing starts); you can run Fathom alongside existing analytics during the trial.
For: Described in their own site structure and copy as for 'European companies' and 'Agencies', and as used by 'Fortune 100s, pioneers of the Open Web, Premier League football clubs, banks, and governments around the world,' as well as 'loads of small and mighty companies.'

Shows proof: Ian Mackey, Huberman Lab: analytics for Huberman Lab run solely on Fathom and are 'incredibly intuitive'; Ruben Gamez, founder of SignWell and Bidsketch: Fathom is 'simple, speedy, and accurate'; Charli Marie, Creative director of ConvertKit, switched to Fathom as an 'ethical analytics tool'; Evan You, creator of Vue.js, uses Fathom for the Vue.js website because it's lightweight and respects user privacy; James Brooks, Head of Enterprise Enablement at Laravel, calls Fathom 'beautiful, fast'; Marshall Shorts, founder of Artfluential, switched to Fathom over visitor privacy; Jon Henshaw, founder of Coywolf, says Fathom respects visitor privacy and is 'a joy to use'; Justin Jackson, Cofounder of Transistor, trusts Fathom as a company that respects privacy; Derrick Reimer, founder of SavvyCal, made Fathom 'part of my default stack'; Jessica Joyce, SEO expert, calls Fathom's dashboard easy to understand 'across all web properties'; Nathalie Lussier, founder of AccessAlly.com, says Fathom protects privacy and doesn't slow sites; Caleb Porzio, creator of Alpine.js, says switching to Fathom made him more attentive to his sites; Joel Gascoigne, CEO of Buffer, says Fathom gives 'all the traffic metrics you could need'; Hero logo wall names Microsoft and Tailwind as customers, alongside 'over a million websites'; Logo wall names GitHub, IBM, New York Times, Vue.js, Bosch, HashiCorp, Aston Villa, Transistor, Bootstrap, SavvyCal, SignWell and Whitney Museum as customers

Counterevidence and its consequence

The adopting body still runs Google Analytics behind a consent mechanism, so the cookieless tool sits alongside rather than replacing the banner. — The purchase rationale is removing the consent banner and the GA risk; this body kept both, so adoption may be additive and lower-value than the hypothesis assumes. Review before prioritising.
The default analytics stack across this government's design-system sites remains the incumbent. — New services inherit a pre-built GTM/GA container, so the alternative is not neutral ground — switching means leaving a supported house standard. Review before prioritising.
The free incumbent is pre-cleared for security and needs no procurement, which a paid tool does. — It names the exact buying obstacle in this candidate's objection: cost plus a procurement and security-assessment step the default option skips entirely. Review before prioritising.

Counterevidence and its consequence

The provisioning capability is gated behind Enterprise and a sales conversation. — The one capability that makes the channel work cannot be self-served or priced in advance, which blocks the build-vs-buy comparison this buyer must run before committing. Review before prioritising.
Scale itself is Enterprise-gated: more than ten sites, the Sites API and the managed proxy all sit above the published plans. — A platform with thousands of customer sites has no published plan to grow into, so every deal starts as a custom contract negotiation. Review before prioritising.
The embedded dashboard leaves per-customer link management and access control to the platform, and rules out password-protected links. — Real but modest engineering work for a platform that already manages tenant auth; it raises integration cost rather than blocking the pattern. Minor condition; does not exclude this audience.
